visuals.title: Quiz
visuals.text: Five questions. Answer along on the cards below the transcript, then hear Marco's answers.

quiz.pause_at: Pause here if you want to think it through

questions.q: Net income is 80, depreciation 20, and receivables go up by 15. What is cash from operations?
questions.explain: 80 + 20 of depreciation − 15 for higher receivables = 85. Higher receivables are cash stuck with customers.
questions.explain_at: Working capital. During the year, customers who owe us

questions.q: Cash from operations is 85 and capex is 50. What is free cash flow?
questions.explain: Free cash flow is cash from operations minus capex: 85 − 50 = 35.
questions.explain_at: And there's one more number to know. Free cash flow

questions.q: A company buys back 30 of its own shares. Where does that go, and with what sign?
questions.explain: Buying back shares returns money to shareholders, so it's a cash outflow in financing.
questions.explain_at: Cash from financing activities: money going to and from lenders and shareholders

questions.q: Inventory goes down by 10 over the year. What happens to cash?
questions.explain: Less cash is stuck on the shelf: an asset going down releases cash.
questions.explain_at: Second trap. An increase in an asset like receivables or inventory uses cash

questions.q: Profits have grown for three years, but cash from operations fell every year. Why is that a warning sign?

options.text: It shows heavy investment in growth
It's paying down debt too quickly

questions.explain: Revenue may be booked before the cash arrives, or receivables are piling up. It's the gap Enron had to hide with the prepays.
questions.explain_at: The classic one is profits going up while cash from operations goes down
